at overnatte.explanation: "At overnatte" means "to stay overnight", for example at a hotel, a hostel or a friend's house. "Vi overnatter på hotel" means "We stay the night at a hotel".

sentence.en: We stay the night at a small hotel.

en onkel.explanation: "En onkel" means "an uncle". Watch the spelling: the "e" drops out before the ending, so "the uncle" is "onklen", not "onkelen". The matching word is "en tante" (an aunt).

sentence.en: My uncle has a big garden.

en ovn.explanation: "En ovn" means "an oven", the one you bake and roast in. Typical phrases are "i ovnen" (in the oven) and "at tænde ovnen" (to turn on the oven). The cooking surface on top is a different word, "en kogeplade" (a hob).

sentence.en: The cake is in the oven.

forms.da: Er der et offentligt toilet her?
forms.en: Is there a public restroom here?

et offentligt toilet.explanation: "Et offentligt toilet" means "a public restroom", one anyone can use, for example in a park or at a station. "Offentligt" (public) ends in "-t" because "toilet" is an et-word; in "det offentlige toilet" (the public restroom) it ends in "-e" instead.

sentence.da: Ved banegården er der et **offentligt toilet**.
sentence.en: At the railway station there is a public restroom.

et ord.explanation: "Et ord" means "a word". "Hvad betyder det ord?" means "What does that word mean?". A dictionary is "en ordbog", literally "a word book".

sentence.en: I don't know that word.

ofte.explanation: "Ofte" means "often". It usually comes right after the word for the action: "Jeg går ofte i skoven" (I often walk in the forest). To ask how often, say "hvor ofte?" (how often?).

sentence.en: We often eat out.

og.explanation: "Og" means "and". The "g" is usually silent, so it sounds like "o". For "both ... and", Danish says "både ... og" (both ... and).

sentence.en: I like coffee and tea.

også.explanation: "Også" means "also" or "too". It usually goes right after the word for the action: "Jeg kan også lide kaffe" (I also like coffee). For "not either", do not say "ikke også"; Danes say "heller ikke" (not either).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **også** have en kop kaffe.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of coffee too.

okay.explanation: "Okay" means "okay", the same word as in English, and Danes use it all the time to agree or show they understand. It is casual but fine in most situations. For a more Danish option, try "fint" (fine) or "i orden" (all right).

sentence.en: See you at five. – Okay!

oksekød.explanation: "Oksekød" means "beef". It is made from "okse" (ox) and "kød" (meat), so it is literally "ox meat". "Kød" on its own means any kind of meat.

sentence.en: I buy beef at the supermarket.

oktober.explanation: "Oktober" means "October". Danish spells it with a "k", unlike English. Like all month names, it is written with a small letter.

sentence.en: There is autumn break in October.

olie.explanation: "Olie" means "oil". It is used for cooking oil and other kinds of oil. For a specific kind, Danes use one-word names like "olivenolie" (olive oil) and "rapsolie" (rapeseed oil).

sentence.en: I fry the meat in oil.

om.explanation: "Om" means "about", as in "en bog om Danmark" (a book about Denmark). It is also used for time ahead: "om en uge" means "in a week". And it can mean "whether": "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming).

sentence.en: The film starts in an hour.

forms.en: In the evening we watch TV.

om aftenen.explanation: "Om aftenen" means "in the evening", as a habit or something that happens every day. For this evening only, use "i aften" (this evening). The ending "-en" in "aftenen" means "the": it is literally "the evening".

sentence.en: We eat together in the evening.

forms.en: I am coming in a little while.
See you in a little while.

om lidt.explanation: "Om lidt" means "in a little while" or "soon". It is a gentle way of saying you will do something soon but not right now. For right now, use "lige nu" (right now).

sentence.en: The food is ready in a little while.

forms.en: I get up in the morning.
In the morning I drink coffee.

om morgenen.explanation: "Om morgenen" means "in the morning", as a regular thing, like what you do every morning. For one particular morning, name the day: "mandag morgen" means "Monday morning".

sentence.en: I go for a run in the morning.

om natten.explanation: "Om natten" means "at night", as something that usually happens. For tonight or last night, use "i nat" (tonight / last night). The ending "-en" in "natten" means "the": it is literally "the night".

sentence.en: It is quiet here at night.

forms.da: Jeg arbejder fem dage om ugen.
forms.en: I work five days a week.

om ugen.explanation: "Om ugen" means "per week" or "a week". It follows a number of times or days: "to gange om ugen" means "twice a week". "Om dagen" (a day) and "om måneden" (a month) work the same way.

sentence.en: I work out three times a week.

omkring.explanation: "Omkring" means "around", for a place or for a rough number: "omkring byen" means "around the town" and "omkring tyve mennesker" means "about twenty people". For moving around, "rundt" (around) is more usual.

sentence.en: We walk around the lake.

ondt.explanation: "Ondt" means "pain" or "hurt". Danish says "Jeg har ondt i maven", literally "I have pain in the stomach", where English says "my stomach hurts". "Det gør ondt" means "It hurts". Do not say "Jeg er ondt".

sentence.en: I have a stomachache.

onsdag.explanation: "Onsdag" means "Wednesday". Like all day names, it starts with a small letter. Use "på onsdag" (on Wednesday, coming up) for the next one, and "om onsdagen" (on Wednesdays) for every week. The "d" is silent but still written.

sentence.en: The children are off on Wednesday.

op.explanation: "Op" means "up" and is used for movement upwards, as in "Kom op!" (Come up!). "Oppe" (up there) is for being in a high place. "Op" is also part of "at stå op" (to get up) and "at vågne op" (to wake up). The opposite is "ned" (down).

sentence.en: I walk up the stairs.

oppe.explanation: "Oppe" means "up there" and says where something is, not movement. For moving upward use "op" (up): "gå op" means "go up". "Er du oppe?" can also ask whether someone is out of bed.

sentence.en: The book is up on the shelf.

optaget.explanation: "Optaget" means "busy" or "taken". Use it for a phone line, a toilet, a seat, or a person who has no time. "Er her optaget?" asks whether a seat is taken. The opposite is "ledig" (free, available).

sentence.en: Is this seat taken?

orange.explanation: "Orange" means "orange", the colour. For the fruit, Danes say "en appelsin" (an orange), not "orange". The colour word never changes, whatever it describes.

sentence.en: Her jacket is orange.

os.explanation: "Os" means "us". Use it when something is done to your group, or after words like "med" (with) and "til" (to). When your group does something, say "vi" (we).

related.en: you (more than one, after words like "med")

sentence.en: Do you want to come with us?

ost.explanation: "Ost" means "cheese". When you mean one kind of cheese, say "en ost": "en fransk ost" means "a French cheese". Without "en" it is cheese in general.

sentence.da: Jeg kan godt lide **ost** på brød.
sentence.en: I like cheese on bread.

otte.explanation: "Otte" means "eight". Be careful not to mix it up with "atten" (eighteen), which starts with an "a", not an "o".

sentence.en: I have eight hours at work.

ottende.explanation: "Ottende" means "eighth". It is used for order, floors and dates: "den ottende marts" means "the eighth of March".

sentence.en: He lives on the eighth floor.

ovenpå.explanation: "Ovenpå" means "upstairs", on the floor above you. It works both for where something is and for going there: "Jeg bor ovenpå" (I live upstairs) and "Jeg går ovenpå" (I go upstairs). The opposite is "nedenunder" (downstairs).

sentence.en: The bedroom is upstairs.

over.explanation: "Over" means "over", "above" or "across". With amounts it means "more than", as in "over to timer" (more than two hours). The opposite is "under" (under, below).

sentence.en: We walk over the bridge.

overalt.explanation: "Overalt" means "everywhere". It usually goes at the end of the sentence, as in "Der er blomster overalt". The opposite is "ingen steder" (nowhere).

sentence.en: There is dirt everywhere.

overskyet.explanation: "Overskyet" means "overcast", with the whole sky covered by cloud. It is stronger than "skyet" (cloudy), which can mean only some clouds. The opposite is "solrig" (sunny).

sentence.en: The sky is overcast today.
